title: CLM and keeper divide the work differently
questions: How is CLM different from keeper?
Who decides what to remember?
Is keeper self-editing?
answer:
CLM lets the working agent edit its own live conversation. The application reads the edited transcript into the next model call. The agent must decide what to retain while doing the task.

A keeper moves that responsibility into the surrounding program: it archives exact old turns, asks the model to refresh short working notes, protects rules and makes the originals searchable. The proxy applies that policy between a client and model server. Neither approach gives the model unlimited simultaneous attention.

title: A small working context with searchable originals
questions: What worked better than compaction?
How do I stop a long-running agent forgetting?
Keeper versus summary versus sliding window
answer:
Keeping exact originals, short working notes and protected rules gave the strongest results in the synthetic long-history tests. On the first 240K-token stream, keeper and proxy each answered 39/39 questions, an archive with pinned rules 35/39, window dropping 23/39 and periodic compaction 20/39. Retrieval alone also answered 39/39 there, where the rule names what it covers. It never found a rule that names nothing (0/16, against 16/16 for the keeper), and it fell behind late in a million-token history.

These are comparisons on the same stream and model, not a general ranking of agents. The proxy has not yet been tested under a real coding or research agent.

title: How the keeper remembers
questions: How does keeper work?
What are keeper notes?
Does the keeper save the original conversation?
answer:
Before old turns leave the working window, the keeper archives them word for word. A separate no-tool call to the same model refreshes short notes about rules, current state and open work. The program restores omitted rules and repeats them beside questions. Search can bring selected original passages back into the live context.

The archive can grow beyond the window. Only the notes, recent turns and retrieved passages occupy the next prompt.

title: Keeper at a million tokens
questions: Did keeper work at one million tokens?
How accurate was the memory proxy?
Did the keeper forget anything?
answer:
On one synthetic million-token stream, the keeper with in-place notes answered all 228 questions in 50 minutes, and the proxy with in-place notes 226 of 228 in 50 minutes. On a second stream the keeper answered 210 of 222. The earlier forms answered 226 of 228 in 83 minutes and, as a proxy, 222 of 228 in 95 minutes. These are one run each, with a small working context and an external archive.

They show that this policy can continue beyond the model's window on this task. They do not establish perfect recall on other tasks or performance under a real coding agent.

title: A file is a record, not automatic model memory
questions: Does saving the transcript mean the model remembers it?
How does an agent read files?
Is a plan file the same as CLM?
answer:
The model sees the prompt supplied in the current call. Saving a transcript or plan on disk does not automatically put its contents into that prompt. Tools must retrieve a passage, load a file or calculate a result from the records.

CLM's transcript has a special role: accepted edits become the next live conversation. Revised CLM also reloads STATE.txt on every call; that text counts against the context budget. Ordinary archive files have neither behavior.

title: Disk storage does not replace GPU working memory
questions: Can I run 200K context with almost no VRAM?
Can the model think directly from an SSD?
Does saving a file offload the KV cache?
Can RAM replace GPU memory?
answer:
Saving text keeps records outside the model. The active numerical state used to generate a reply still needs an execution engine and working memory. For this model, a 200,000-token attention cache is estimated at about 12.2 GiB across the two GPUs, before other state and working memory.

An offloading engine could trade transfers or CPU work for capacity, but active RAM or disk offload was not benchmarked in these runs. Reading a file between model calls is a different operation.

title: Prefix caching saves repeated reading
questions: Does caching make the model write faster?
What is prefix caching?
Why is the first token faster?
answer:
Prefix caching reuses the numerical work for an unchanged beginning of the prompt. In the 30K-token test, a matching cached prefix reduced time to first token from about 11.4 seconds to 0.8 seconds. Writing speed stayed around 89 tokens per second.

It saves repeated reading; it does not shrink the live history or give the model more memory. A cold read still has to process the prompt, and edits limit which cached prefix can be reused.

title: Use code for exact bookkeeping
questions: Which approach was fastest on the ledger?
Why were files and code faster than CLM?
Should the model calculate every update?
answer:
In the 121K-token ledger test, files and code answered all 24 questions in about 1.9 minutes. Code maintained exact totals outside the live prompt, so the model did not need to repeatedly read and rewrite the whole ledger.

This works especially well when the task has precise update rules. It does not establish the same advantage for open-ended conversation or prose understanding, where deciding what matters is harder.

title: Summaries can lose details that later matter
questions: Why not just summarize everything?
Is compaction lossless?
Can summaries recover forgotten details?
answer:
A summary replaces earlier text with a shorter account. It can preserve useful state, but a summary alone cannot recover a detail it left out. Keeping the original records makes later checking possible.

Summaries matched the archive on the smaller retention test, with all 36 answers correct, but took longer. Whole-history reading led on the separate 56-question chat-memory test. The best choice depends on the task and whether the original source fits comfortably.

title: Download and use the keeper proxy
questions: Can I use the keeper myself?
How do I install ctxkeeper?
Does the proxy work with my agent?
Which coding agents work with ctxkeeper?
answer:
ctxkeeper is a free, public-domain proxy that applies the keeper between your agent and any OpenAI-compatible model server, such as vLLM or llama.cpp. Install it with pip or Docker, start it with the address of your server, and point your agent at the proxy instead.

It works with programs that use Chat Completions, send their whole history each time and have their own trimming turned off. Twelve open-source coding agents were run through it on a 40-bug code-repair task, among them Cline, Goose, OpenHands, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, Mistral Vibe, Hermes Agent and mini-swe-agent; ten of the eleven that ran fixed 39 or 40 of the 40 bugs. Results were measured on one model family and one machine.
